catalog_quote: To distinguish these hypotheses the perception experiment was repeated with speakers of Cakchiquel, a related Mayan language, which has fixed final stress and no phonemic length. ... Cakchiquel speakers in associating greater length with stress, expect that the final syllable (the normal location of stress) will be longer than any other syllable in the word.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog StressTyp2 record for Cakchiquel is final stress = fixed final stress; Townsend states exactly that (accent always on the last syllable), adding only the Spanish-loan exemption and an observation that stress shifts rightward onto added suffix syllables. Variety described: San Juan Comalapa (Chimaltenango, Guatemala), stated to be readily understood from Solola to San Juan Sacatepequez.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent is invariably on the final syllable of native Cakchiquel words; when a suffix adds a syllable the stress moves off the root onto the new final syllable (with attendant root-vowel change e -> a in one verb class).
new_statements.exceptions: Spanish loanwords are exempt from the final-accent rule (they keep their Spanish accent). No other exceptions given.
new_statements.identity_note: Townsend's grammar is explicitly based on the Cakchiquel of San Juan Comalapa, Department of Chimaltenango, Guatemala (Introduction para. 1, p. 9), which he says is readily understood from Solola to San Juan Sacatepequez 'but each town varies somewhat'. The orthography is Spanish-based (pre-ALMG); the work is a 1926 manuscript published in 1961 as a historical document with a foreword by K. L. Pike.

tone_statements.quote: a. Stress: Kaqchikel is a word-final stress language. Lax //a//, i.e., /ä/, as the nucleus of a lexical monosyllabic root (jäl, chäj, kär, kyäq, säq, q'än, räx, etc.) is therefore always stressed if not derived (saqsöj 'whitish'), nor compounded (saqmoloj 'egg'). In such cases, stress proceeds rightwards to the suffixal or last compound word's syllable (i.e. saqsöj, saqmoloj). || Moreover, as stress regularly falls on the last syllable in Kaqchikel, all suffixal lax vowels are actually stressed nuclei, so that unlike languages such as Portuguese or Russian, laxity has nothing to do with prosodic intensity or strength constraints in Mayan languages. || the length correlation of Proto-Mayan (VLC) did shift to a Tense/Lax Contrast (TLVC) at the segmental level, but it still smoulders under the surface of actual duration and a High tone feature associated with the lax vowel.

tone_statements.summary: Stress: word-final, on the last syllable of the word including derivational suffixes and compounds (saqsöj, saqmoloj); domain = the (compound) word. Secondary stress: not mentioned. Weight: stress is not tied to vowel laxity/length ('laxity has nothing to do with prosodic intensity or strength constraints'); tense long //aa// and lax //a// both occur stressed. Exceptions: none stated. Tone: no ton

audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-strict' final stress (final stress) is correct: the Berinstein 1979 quotations are verbatim at pp. vi, 47, 52 of the eScholarship scan (now saved to our files; previously only a /tmp copy existed), and the held 1997 OKMA reference grammar (Rukemik ri Kaqchikel Chi', pp. 20-21, sec. 'Acento') states the same rule explicitly for radical, derived and compound words with directional enclitics attracting the stress, as do the held Bennett 2016 (p.495), Bennett 2018 (fn.7: word-final, no secondary stress) and ALMG 2004, and the newly downloaded Nelson 2020 acoustic check. No source contradicts. The weakness is only in the pin: the record's deciding citation is a 1979 perception thesis reached through StressTyp2/Gordon 2002, with empty quote/cite/grade fields on the main record, while a native-speaker reference grammar we already hold gives the rule first-hand. Action: re-pin

sources.quote: El Kaqchikel se caracteriza por tener acento fijo en una sílaba determinada. El acento es agudo, lo que significa que la acentuación siempre va a recaer en la sílaba final de la palabra (radical, derivada o compuesta por dos raíces unidas o dos palabras separadas). Al agregar enclíticos a los verbos y estativos (como direccionales), el acento tiende a caer sobre éstos. [...] El acento fijo en la estructura de la palabra no requiere de representación ortográfica (tilde) porque su ubicación es predecible y su lugar es único (sílaba final). [...] El acento agudo del Kaqchikel no resistió al acento grave (penúltima sílaba) y [...] de los préstamos lexicales del castellano. [...] Ejemplos: kaxa caja, xara jarro, anma ánima/alma. Algunas variantes tienen dos o tres palabras propias [que se] exceptúan de la regla aguda. Entre ellas tenemos [...] señora y señor que son nana, y tata, respectivamente, que tienen el acento [en] la primera sílaba. Las demás variantes dialectales tienen nan y tat, ésta es la forma más corta del sustantivo del cual se originó (tata'aj, padre). Comalapa [tiene] el adjetivo janila, mucho. sources.quote: 'The preceding examples show that Kaqchikel does in fact place main word stress on the final syllable of the word. However, there are a few exceptions ... Word-final stress is by far the most common pattern for native vocabulary' -- janila /xanila/ 'very' has penultimate stress (Fig. 6); Spanish loans variable (ruxumprente); 'while Kaqchikel overwhelmingly prefers word-final stress, there is no absolute restriction against other patterns.'
sources.locator: sec. 3.1 'Word stress', pp. 75-77 (acoustic examples, 1-4 syllable words, Figs. 2-7)
sources.note: Only acoustic verification of Kaqchikel word-final stress found (pitch/intensity tracks on 1-4 syllable words); documents the janila and loanword exceptions instrumentally.

sources.citation: Bennett, Ryan. 2018. Recursive prosodic words in Kaqchikel (Mayan). Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 3(1): 67, 1-33. doi:10.5334/gjgl.550
sources.quote: the domain of stress in Kaqchikel is the prosodic word, but high-attaching prefixes are uniformly unstressed (stress is basically restricted to word-final position in Kaqchikel; see Bennett 2016 and references there). [...] compounds may consist of multiple ωs, each bearing an independent stress prominence (26). [fn. 7:] Secondary stress has never been reported for Kaqchikel [...] There are two phonotactic patterns which diagnose stress in Kaqchikel: the presence of lax vowels, and the presence of a [ʔC] cluster. These are absolutely limited to stressed, word-final syllables [...] it seems safest to assume that there is no word-level secondary stress at all in Kaqchikel.
